title: How is data consistency handled in a distributed microservices architecture (strong vs eventual, Saga, event-driven, 2PC, outbox)?
shortTitle: How data consistency is handled in distributed microservices

s1_definition.profdef: In a distributed microservices architecture each service owns its own database, so a single database transaction can no longer span a multi-service business operation, and you must choose a consistency model deliberately. Strong consistency means every reader sees the latest write immediately and is achievable within one service's database; eventual consistency means replicas and downstream services converge to the same value after a short delay. Across services you coordinate changes with the Saga pattern (a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions on failure), driven by events published reliably through the transactional outbox pattern, generally preferring Sagas and eventual consistency over the blocking two-phase commit (2PC/XA) protocol.
s1_definition.analogy: Inside one department of National Bank of India, the ledger is kept perfectly balanced at every instant — that is strong consistency. But when Rajesh's transfer touches the accounts department, the fraud department, and the notification department, there is no single pen that writes all three books in one stroke. Instead each department does its own step and hands a note to the next: debit here, check fraud there, settle, notify. If a later step fails, earlier departments reverse their entry with a correcting note — that is a Saga with compensations. The notes are dropped reliably into a mailbox so one can never be lost even if a department crashes mid-write — that is the outbox. For a few seconds the books across departments may not match, but they settle to agreement — that is eventual consistency.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep money strongly consistent inside one service, and stitch multi-service operations together with Sagas, reliable events via the outbox, and eventual consistency — not with blocking two-phase commit.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** In a distributed microservices architecture each service owns its own database, so a single database transaction can no longer span a multi-service business operation, and you must choose a consistency model deliberately. Strong consistency means every reader sees the latest write immediately and is achievable within one service's database; eventual consistency means replicas and downstream services converge to the same value after a short delay. Across services you coordinate changes with the Saga pattern (a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions on failure), driven by events published reliably through the transactional outbox pattern, generally preferring Sagas and eventual consistency over the blocking two-phase commit (2PC/XA) protocol.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Inside one department of National Bank of India, the ledger is kept perfectly balanced at every instant — that is strong consistency. But when Rajesh's transfer touches the accounts department, the fraud department, and the notification department, there is no single pen that writes all three books in one stroke. Instead each department does its own step and hands a note to the next: debit here, check fraud there, settle, notify. If a later step fails, earlier departments reverse their entry with a correcting note — that is a Saga with compensations. The notes are dropped reliably into a mailbox so one can never be lost even if a department crashes mid-write — that is the outbox. For a few seconds the books across departments may not match, but they settle to agreement — that is eventual consistency.

**One line to remember:** Keep money strongly consistent inside one service, and stitch multi-service operations together with Sagas, reliable events via the outbox, and eventual consistency — not with blocking two-phase commit.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the models. Strong consistency guarantees that once a write commits, every subsequent read sees it; this is the ACID behavior you get within a single relational database and is exactly what you want for the actual money inside one service. Eventual consistency guarantees only that, given no new updates, all copies converge to the same value after some delay; it is what you get across services and across replicas, and it is perfectly acceptable for derived data like statements, dashboards, and search indexes.

Within a single service you keep strong consistency the ordinary way, with a local ACID transaction and optimistic or pessimistic locking. The hard part is a business operation that spans services, because there is no longer a shared transaction manager you want to rely on.

The classic textbook answer is two-phase commit (2PC), usually via XA. A coordinator asks every participant to prepare and vote, and if all vote yes it tells them to commit. It does give atomicity across resources, but it is a blocking, synchronous protocol: participants hold locks from the prepare phase until the final decision, and if the coordinator crashes after everyone votes yes, participants are stuck holding locks indefinitely. It also scales poorly and couples availability to the slowest participant. For these reasons most microservice architectures avoid 2PC for cross-service business operations.

The preferred approach is the Saga pattern: model the operation as a sequence of local transactions, one per service, each publishing an event that triggers the next step; if a later step fails, you run compensating transactions that semantically undo the earlier committed steps. There is no global lock and no global transaction, so it scales and stays available, at the price of eventual consistency and the need to design compensations. Sagas come in two coordination styles: choreography, where services react to each other's events with no central brain, and orchestration, where a central orchestrator explicitly drives each step and issues compensations, which is easier to observe and is preferred for complex flows.

This is event-driven, and events must be published reliably, which exposes the dual-write problem: if a service commits its database change and then publishes an event as two separate steps, a crash in between leaves them inconsistent — the money moved but no one was told, or vice versa. The transactional outbox pattern solves this: in the same local transaction that changes the business data, you also insert an event row into an outbox table, so both commit atomically; a separate relay then reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka, either by polling or by Change Data Capture (for example Debezium tailing the database log), giving at-least-once delivery. Because delivery is at-least-once, consumers must be idempotent, typically by tracking processed event IDs.

A senior engineer ties it together: choose consistency per data type, not globally. The authoritative money stays strongly consistent inside the owning service. Everything cross-service is a Saga driven by reliably-published events through an outbox, converging to eventual consistency, with idempotent consumers and a reconciliation job as a safety net. Reserve 2PC for the rare case of two truly transactional resources under one operator, and reach for it only when eventual consistency is genuinely unacceptable, which across independent services it almost never is.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India processes a transfer from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001) that spans three services — accounts (debit/credit), fraud (risk check), and notification. There is no single database transaction across all three, so consistency must be engineered.

Problem 1 — If the account service debits Rajesh and then the fraud service rejects the transfer, Rajesh has lost money for a transfer that did not happen. We cannot wrap all three in one ACID transaction. This is exactly where a Saga with compensating actions applies: on fraud rejection, run a compensating credit that returns Rajesh's money.

Problem 2 — The account service must tell the others what happened by publishing an event, but if it commits the debit and then crashes before publishing, the money moved and nobody knows. This is the dual-write problem, solved by the transactional outbox: write the balance change and an outbox event row in one local transaction, then a relay publishes it, so the event can never be lost.

Problem 3 — The notification and statement views are allowed to lag by a few seconds, and events may be delivered more than once on retry. This is eventual consistency with at-least-once delivery, handled by idempotent consumers that ignore an event ID they have already processed.

What the code will do: a runnable demo implements an orchestrated Saga. `TransferOrchestrator.execute()` runs step 1 (debit via `AccountService`, writing an outbox row in the same local transaction), step 2 (fraud check via `FraudService`), and on fraud rejection runs the compensating credit. An `OutboxRelay` drains the outbox and publishes events; a `NotificationConsumer` processes them idempotently, ignoring duplicates. The demo shows one successful transfer and one that is rejected by fraud and fully compensated, proving money is never lost.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: first a Rs.50000 transfer (below the Rs.500000 fraud threshold), then a Rs.800000 transfer (above it), both from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001).

Step 1: For the Rs.50000 transfer, `TransferOrchestrator.execute()` runs step one. `AccountService.debitAndCredit()` debits Rajesh to Rs.950,000, credits Priya to Rs.300,000, and in the same local transaction inserts a TransferDebited row into the outbox. Both the money change and the event are committed atomically — no dual-write gap.

Step 2: The fraud service approves Rs.50000 because it is below the threshold. The Saga completes; the money change stands.

Step 3: The outbox relay drains and publishes the event to the notification consumer, which sends an SMS and records the event ID as processed.

Step 4: The relay drains a second time, re-delivering the same event (simulating at-least-once). The notification consumer sees the event ID is already processed and ignores it — idempotency prevents a duplicate SMS.

Step 5: For the Rs.800000 transfer, step one again debits Rajesh (now to Rs.150,000) and credits Priya, writing an outbox row in one local transaction.

Step 6: The fraud service rejects Rs.800000 because it exceeds the threshold. The orchestrator runs the compensating transaction: Rajesh is credited back Rs.800,000 (restored to Rs.950,000) and Priya debited back. The Saga ends in a consistent state — no money was lost even though there was never a global transaction.

Final output:

```
12:00:01 INFO    === SUCCESS Saga: Rs.50,000 (below fraud threshold) ===
12:00:01 INFO    [ACCOUNT] debit SAV2001 credit CUR3001 Rs.50000 + outbox row (1 txn)
12:00:01 INFO    [SAGA] completed; SAV2001 balance now Rs.950000
12:00:01 INFO    [NOTIFY] SMS sent for TransferDebited SAV2001->CUR3001:50000
12:00:01 INFO    === FAILURE Saga: Rs.800,000 (fraud rejects → compensate) ===
12:00:01 INFO    [ACCOUNT] debit SAV2001 credit CUR3001 Rs.800000 + outbox row (1 txn)
12:00:01 SEVERE  [FRAUD] rejected Rs.800000 — running compensation
12:00:01 WARNING [ACCOUNT] COMPENSATE: returned Rs.800000 to SAV2001
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Data consistency in microservices begins with accepting a hard truth: because each service owns its own database, a single ACID transaction can no longer span a multi-service business operation, so I choose a consistency model deliberately rather than pretending the monolith's guarantees still hold. Strong consistency, where every read sees the latest write immediately, is achievable inside one service's database and is exactly what I use for the authoritative money. Eventual consistency, where downstream services and replicas converge to the same value after a short delay, is what I get across services, and it is perfectly fine for derived data like statements, notifications, and search indexes.

For a business operation that spans services, the textbook option is two-phase commit over XA, where a coordinator asks every participant to prepare and vote and then commit. It does provide cross-resource atomicity, but it is a blocking, synchronous protocol: participants hold locks from the prepare phase until the final decision, and if the coordinator crashes after everyone votes yes, they can hold those locks indefinitely, so it scales poorly and ties availability to the slowest participant. That is why I avoid 2PC for cross-service operations and instead use the Saga pattern. A Saga models the operation as a sequence of local transactions, one per service, each publishing an event that triggers the next, and if a later step fails I run compensating transactions that semantically undo the earlier committed steps. There is no global lock and no global transaction, so it stays scalable and available, at the cost of eventual consistency and the need to design compensations.

Because Sagas are event-driven, the events must be published reliably, and that exposes the dual-write problem — if a service commits its database change and then publishes an event as two separate steps, a crash in between leaves the money moved but nobody notified. I solve that with the transactional outbox pattern: in the very same local transaction that changes the business data, I also insert an event row into an outbox table, so both commit atomically, and a separate relay publishes those rows to Kafka, either by polling or by change data capture with Debezium tailing the database log. Delivery is at-least-once, so my consumers are idempotent, tracking processed event IDs and ignoring duplicates.

I built exactly this for transfers at National Bank of India. A transfer from Rajesh to Priya spans the account, fraud, and notification services, with no shared transaction. The orchestrator first runs a local transaction in the account service that debits, credits, and writes an outbox event together, then calls the fraud service. When fraud rejects a large transfer, the orchestrator runs a compensating credit that returns Rajesh's money, so even though there was never a global transaction, no rupee is ever lost. The outbox relay publishes reliably, and because it is at-least-once, the notification consumer dedupes by event ID so a retried delivery never sends a second SMS, and the statement read model simply converges a few seconds later.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is this: keep the money strongly consistent inside the owning service, coordinate multi-service operations with a Saga and compensating actions rather than blocking two-phase commit, publish the triggering events reliably with the transactional outbox so a write and a publish can never drift apart, make every consumer idempotent, and accept eventual consistency for everything derived.
